blocks.heading: Pebble selection, size and shape
blocks.text: A pebble investigation needs an explicit selection method and consistent measurements. Define the stretch of beach and the comparison being tested. Systematic sampling can select positions at stated intervals from a stated start; random sampling uses a chance procedure linked to eligible positions; stratified sampling selects within relevant groups under a declared allocation. These methods address different coverage issues. Choosing the nearest attractive pebble is not random. A quadrat placed at each sample point marks the area from which pebbles are chosen. Size is measured with a ruler, callipers or pebbleometer; a roundness chart classifies shape.

blocks.text:
At each selected position, apply a consistent rule for choosing a pebble and state how an absent suitable pebble will be handled. Measure the agreed axis, commonly the longest axis for a simple size comparison, using suitable units and a consistent instrument. Assess shape with the same supplied roundness scale. Size and roundness are different variables; a large stone can be rounded and a small one angular. Record both against the position rather than assuming that one predicts the other.

![Pebble sampling positions, longest-axis measurement and roundness scale](../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.5-048-PROC-answer.png)

blocks.text: Repeat or cross-check measurements where feasible, and avoid selective replacement of inconvenient observations. An observer comparison can reveal inconsistent use of a shape scale. A larger sample may improve coverage but does not repair a biased selection rule. Interpret the pattern using the sampled places and date, considering sediment sources, transport and local conditions. Attrition can help explain rounding, but a fresh sediment input or selective sampling can create exceptions. This connects field evidence to the erosion and transport mechanisms without claiming that every pebble’s complete history is known from its appearance.
